c.entradas.nibiru.nombre_original: nēberu (Akkadian, 'crossing, passage, ford, place of crossing'; also 'ferry'), written MUL né-bé-ru
c.entradas.nibiru.fecha_texto: As an astronomical term it appears in the Enuma Elish (late 2nd millennium BC), in the MUL.APIN compendium (oldest copies c. 686 BC, older content) and in Neo-Assyrian and late astrological texts and commentaries.
c.entradas.nibiru.resumen: In Akkadian, nēberu means 'crossing' or 'passage', for example the place where a river is forded. In astronomy it designates a point or a star in the sky associated with Marduk, which most texts identify with the planet Jupiter in a particular position. No cuneiform text describes a hidden planet or a body approaching the Earth.
c.entradas.nibiru.interpretacion:
What the texts say: the word comes from the verb ebēru, 'to cross', and in everyday life it designates fords and ferryboats. In astronomy, MUL.APIN describes a great star that 'divides the sky in two' and calls it 'the star of Marduk, Nēberu, Jupiter'. That is, the planet when observed in a certain position or at a certain time of year, associated with the month of Tashritu and the equinox. Other texts, such as astrological fragments from Nineveh, also call Mercury Nēberu in certain circumstances. That is why many specialists understand Nēberu as a transit point in the sky, occupied by the visible celestial body that 'crosses' it, rather than as the fixed name of a single body. Johannes Koch (1991) and others discuss its exact identification, which remains debated in its details (Jupiter, Mercury or a point in the sky near the equinox), but it is always a matter of visible, known objects.

In the Enuma Elish, Marduk fixes the positions of the stars in Tablet V, and Tablet VII gives Nēberu as one of his fifty names: the star that 'holds the crossing' of heaven and earth and controls the course of the stars. It is a theological identification of the god with his star, not the description of a twelfth planet. The idea of Nibiru as a planet with a 3,600-year orbit that collided with Tiamat and was inhabited by the Anunnaki comes from Zecharia Sitchin (1976). It has no basis in the cuneiform sources, and Assyriologists and astronomers reject it. The modern prophecies of a collision with 'Nibiru' (2003, 2012, 2017) have nothing to do with Babylonian astronomy.
c.entradas.nibiru.detalles.0: Root: ebēru, 'to cross'; in everyday texts nēberu designates a ford or a ferryboat.
c.entradas.nibiru.detalles.1: MUL.APIN, Tablet I: 'the star of Marduk, Nēberu, Jupiter' when it 'divides the sky'.
c.entradas.nibiru.detalles.2: Enuma Elish, Tablet VII: Nēberu is one of Marduk's fifty names and is 'his star'.
c.entradas.nibiru.detalles.3: Some fragments from Nineveh (for example K.6174) identify Mercury as Nēberu in certain positions.
c.entradas.nibiru.detalles.4: The figure of 3,600 years (one sar) is a number of the sexagesimal system that the King List uses for reigns. No text presents it as an orbital period.
c.entradas.nibiru.fuentes_primarias.0: MUL.APIN compendium (copies from Assur and Nineveh, c. 686 BC onward)
c.entradas.nibiru.fuentes_primarias.1: Enuma Elish, Tablets V and VII
c.entradas.nibiru.fuentes_primarias.2: Astrological texts and commentaries from the Library of Ashurbanipal
c.entradas.dilmun.fecha_texto: Mentioned from the protoliterate period (c. 3000 BC) to the 1st millennium BC. The archaeological peak of the Dilmun culture in Bahrain is c. 2050–1700 BC.
c.entradas.dilmun.resumen: Dilmun was a real region of the Persian Gulf, identified with the island of Bahrain and the eastern coast of Arabia. It was a major center of trade between Mesopotamia, Magan (Oman) and Meluhha (Indus Valley). In the myths it appears as a pure, primordial land.
c.entradas.dilmun.interpretacion:
Dilmun has two faces. It was a historical place of trade, above all in copper, as the texts of the merchants of Ur show, and at the same time a mythical space. In 'Enki and Ninhursag' it is a land where neither sickness nor death existed, and in the Sumerian flood story it is the place to which the immortal Ziusudra withdraws.

Archaeology (Qal'at al-Bahrain, the Barbar temple and the thousands of burial mounds of Bahrain) confirms the existence of a distinct culture. Sargon of Akkad boasted that ships from Dilmun docked at his capital.
c.entradas.dilmun.detalles.0: It is identified with Bahrain thanks to cuneiform inscriptions found there, such as the 'Durand stone', from the 18th century BC.
c.entradas.dilmun.detalles.1: It was an intermediary in the copper trade from Magan.
c.entradas.dilmun.detalles.2: Bahrain preserves large Bronze Age burial mound fields, a World Heritage Site since 2019.
c.entradas.dilmun.detalles.3: In the myths it is the place where Ziusudra receives eternal life.
c.entradas.dilmun.fuentes_primarias.0: Excavations at Qal'at al-Bahrain and the Barbar temple
c.entradas.dilmun.fuentes_primarias.1: Texts of the merchants of Ur (Old Babylonian)
c.entradas.kur-inframundo.nombre_origina: kur (Sumerian, 'mountain, foreign land, Underworld'); arallû, erṣetu, 'land of no return' (Akkadian)
c.entradas.kur-inframundo.fecha_texto: These conceptions are documented from the 3rd millennium BC. The main literary descriptions are Old Babylonian and from the 1st millennium BC.
c.entradas.kur-inframundo.resumen: The Mesopotamian Underworld is a dark place beneath the earth to which all the dead go. There they eat dust and drink muddy water. It is ruled by Ereshkigal and, later, Nergal, and it is entered through seven gates.
c.entradas.kur-inframundo.interpretacion:
The word kur also means 'mountain' and 'foreign land': for the inhabitants of the plain, what was distant and hostile merged with the world of the dead. There is no moral judgment and no rewards and punishments as in later religions. There are, however, differences depending on the funerary rites received: the dead person with no descendants to make offerings (kispu) suffers more, as described in 'Bilgames, Enkidu and the Netherworld'.

Mesopotamian cosmology distinguishes heaven, earth, the Apsu and, further down, the Underworld. In some texts the Anunnaki act as its judges.
c.entradas.kur-inframundo.detalles.0: It is entered through seven gates, with a gatekeeper, Neti (Bidu in Akkadian).
c.entradas.kur-inframundo.detalles.1: The dead are clothed in feathers 'like birds' and eat dust, according to the Descent of Ishtar.
c.entradas.kur-inframundo.detalles.2: The galla demons are in charge of taking people to the Underworld.
c.entradas.kur-inframundo.detalles.3: Tablet XII of Gilgamesh describes the fate of different kinds of dead.
c.entradas.zigurat.nombre_original: ziqqurratu (Akkadian, from zaqāru, 'to raise'); in Sumerian, u6-nir
c.entradas.zigurat.fecha_texto: Raised temple platforms exist from the Ubaid and Uruk periods. The classic stepped ziggurat appears in Ur III (c. 2100 BC) and is built down to the Neo-Babylonian Empire.
c.entradas.zigurat.resumen: A stepped tower of mud brick and baked brick crowned by a temple. It rose at the center of the main Mesopotamian cities. It was the raised 'house' of the city's patron god.
c.entradas.zigurat.interpretacion:
Scholars interpret the ziggurat as a link between heaven and earth. This is indicated by names such as Etemenanki ('House of the foundation of heaven and earth') in Babylon or Duranki ('bond between heaven and earth') for Nippur. It also served royal prestige: the kings of Ur III built them at Ur, Uruk, Eridu and Nippur.

They were not tombs, unlike the Egyptian pyramids, nor were they landing platforms. They were solid masses of mud brick with no interior chambers, with stairways leading to a high temple. The Etemenanki of Babylon is often considered the inspiration for the biblical story of the Tower of Babel.
c.entradas.zigurat.detalles.0: The ziggurat of Ur was built by Ur-Nammu and Shulgi, c. 2100 BC, and excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s.
c.entradas.zigurat.detalles.1: The Etemenanki of Babylon, dedicated to Marduk, measured about 91 m per side at the base according to the 'Esagila Tablet'.
c.entradas.zigurat.detalles.2: Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II restored it in the 6th century BC.
c.entradas.zigurat.detalles.3: The 'White Temple' of Uruk, on a terrace dedicated to An, dates to the Uruk period (c. 3500–3100 BC).
c.entradas.disco-alado.nombre_original: Winged sun disk (iconographic motif; no certain Akkadian term)
c.entradas.disco-alado.fecha_texto: The motif reached Mesopotamia from Egypt by way of Syria and Anatolia in the 2nd millennium BC. It is common in Middle Assyrian and Neo-Assyrian art (13th–7th centuries BC) and was inherited by the Achaemenids.
c.entradas.disco-alado.resumen: A disk with outspread wings, sometimes with a bearded human figure inside it or with a feathered tail. It appears above Assyrian royal scenes as a symbol of divine protection.
c.entradas.disco-alado.interpretacion:
The motif is Egyptian in origin: the winged sun disk of Horus of Behdet. From there it passed to the Levant, to the Hittites and to Mitanni, and finally to Assyria. In Assyria it is debated whom it represents. The traditional interpretation attributes it to Ashur, especially when it holds a figure with a bow, but Black and Green and other scholars maintain that it is often Shamash, the sun god. The British Museum and the Metropolitan Museum describe the figure as 'Ashur or Shamash', that is, of uncertain identification.

The Achaemenids adapted it (for example at Persepolis and Behistun), and it is usually associated with Ahura Mazda, although that too is debated. The academic reading sees it as an emblem of the divine presence and favor that protect the king, not as a depiction of a flying machine or a planet.
c.entradas.disco-alado.detalles.0: It appears above the king in the reliefs of Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud (9th century BC).
c.entradas.disco-alado.detalles.1: In some cases the figure in the disk draws a bow, paralleling the king in battle.
c.entradas.disco-alado.detalles.2: The motif comes from Egypt, by way of Syria and Mitanni.
c.entradas.disco-alado.detalles.3: In Persia it appears on the Behistun relief of Darius I (c. 520 BC).
c.entradas.disco-alado.fuentes_primarias: Reliefs from the Northwest Palace at Nimrud (British Museum)
c.entradas.lamassu.nombre_original: lamassu / aladlammû (Akkadian); in Sumerian, lamma; the male spirit is also called šēdu
c.entradas.lamassu.fecha_texto: The great gateway sculptures are Neo-Assyrian (9th–7th centuries BC). The concept of the protective goddess Lamma is Sumerian (3rd millennium BC).
c.entradas.lamassu.resumen: Stone colossi with the body of a bull or a lion, bird's wings and a human head with a horned tiara, which guarded the gates of Assyrian palaces. They were protective spirits that warded off evil.
c.entradas.lamassu.interpretacion:
Originally, Lamma was a Sumerian protective goddess who appears on seals presenting worshipers to the gods. In Assyria, the hybrid male protective figures, which combine the strength of the bull, the swiftness of the bird and human intelligence, were placed in pairs at gateways as apotropaic guardians.

A well-known peculiarity is that many have five legs: in this way they appear to be standing still when seen from the front and striding when seen from the side. The horned tiara indicates their divine nature. Their function, according to the inscriptions and ritual texts, is magical and protective.
c.entradas.lamassu.detalles.0: Those of Ashurnasirpal II from Nimrud are in the British Museum and the Metropolitan Museum.
c.entradas.lamassu.detalles.1: Those of Sargon II from Dur-Sharrukin (Khorsabad) are in the Louvre and the Oriental Institute in Chicago.
c.entradas.lamassu.detalles.2: Many have five legs so that they can be seen properly from two viewpoints.
c.entradas.lamassu.detalles.3: In 2015, the Islamic State destroyed several lamassu at Nineveh and Nimrud.
